concepts: Spiderweb Software; small team, long-running indie RPGs
Non-hits focus; sustainable middle-class income
Postmortem-style career reflection as a career canvas
sections.description: Jeff Vogel introduces Spiderweb Software, frames the talk as a career postmortem rather than a single-game postmortem, and outlines the studio’s philosophy of making turn-based, dialogue-heavy RPGs with a sustainable, middle-class income rather than chasing blockbuster hits.
sections.title: Origins, company philosophy, and the long view

concepts: Shareware as a marketing model in 1994
Demos spread via BBS, AOL, Prodigy, magazines, mall kiosks
Money flow: checks, postal money orders, and the early credit-card barrier
sections.description: Describes the 1994-1995 shareware approach, the distribution ecosystem before broad consumer internet, and the friction of monetizing demos during that era (full game price, mailing payments, and the steps to accept credit cards).
sections.title: Shareware era and practical distribution

concepts: Copy from favorite games to form a cohesive whole

Ship something tangible even if flawed; ‘good enough’ is a strategic target
sections.description: Explains the practical, non-artsiness of Vogel’s process: basing a game on loved inspirations, reusing code/assets, and committing to shipping when the product is sufficiently complete rather than perfect.
sections.title: Creative process, lean development, and the ‘25% redo’ rule

concepts: Going independent from Fantasoft; accepting credit cards

concepts: Indie games grow because audiences like the underdog story
the value of being approachable and honest with fans

concepts: Years of back catalog revenue

sections.description: Wraps with pragmatic maxims about shipping cadence, continual growth, and wise risk-taking, ending with Steve Martin’s pee-test analogy and the notion that making it as an indie is possible but hard.
sections.title: Closing reflections and big-picture advice

summary: Jeff Vogel of Spiderweb Software offers a long-range, no-nonsense retrospective on building a sustainable indie RPG studio across more than two decades. Grounded in a refusal to chase ‘hits,’ he explains a philosophy of lean development, back-catalog leverage, and remastering as a business strategy, paired with careful cash flow and fan-base cultivation. The talk traces early shareware distribution in the 1990s, the challenges of launching Exile and Avernum titles, the shift to independent publishing with in-house payment processing, and the evolution through Geneforge, Avernum remasters, and new IPs. Vogel emphasizes luck, persistence, the value of owning your source, and the necessity of protecting one’s mental bandwidth from critics while remaining likable to fans. Throughout, he balances practical advice (pricing, contracts, accounting, art workflows) with candid humility about the risks and uncertainties of a long career in an industry that Nobody “knows” yet, while underscoring that quality, consistency, and a loyal fan base can sustain a life as a ‘humble toy maker’ in a brutally competitive market.
title: Failing to Fail: The Spiderweb Software Way
topics: Credit card processing for indie games
North Star and long-term career planning
